fund-java/24-bean-validation-in-depth/01.instructions:
**Skills:** Bean Validation · reflection · property paths  
**Level:** ★★★

**Interview prompt.** "Our order API accepts an order whose second line has a blank SKU, although `OrderLine.sku` is `@NotBlank`. Explain how a Bean Validation engine walks an object, then build a small one."

**Why it matters.** A validator reads each component's annotations, applies them, and descends into a nested object or into a list's elements ONLY where `@Valid` asks it to. Each built-in constraint treats `null` as valid except the NotNull family. Violations carry a property path, so the client can mark the right field.

**Your task.** Implement `static List<String> validate(Record root)` for the given annotations (on record components). Return every violation as `"<path>: <message>"`, sorted:
- `@NotNull`: a `null` value gives `must not be null`
- `@NotBlank`: `null` or a blank string gives `must not be blank`
- `@Size(min, max)`: for a non-null value, its length (a `String`) or size (a `Collection`) outside `min..max` gives `size must be between <min> and <max>`
- `@Min(v)`: a non-null number below `v` gives `must be at least <v>`
- `@Valid`: for a non-null record, validate it with the path prefix `<name>.`; for a non-null list, validate each record element with the prefix `<name>[<index>].`
- the path of a component is its name, after any prefix

**Worked example.** An order whose `items` are `[Item("tea", 1), Item("", 0)]` gives `["items[1].qty: must be at least 1", "items[1].sku: must not be blank"]`.
hints: A record can describe its own components, and each component carries the annotations written on it. The walk only goes deeper where one particular annotation says so.

For every component read its value, apply each annotation it carries, letting the size and minimum rules ignore a missing value, and descend into a nested record or into each record in a list only when it is marked for cascading, extending the path as you go.

Loop over the record components, read each value through its accessor, add a message for each broken rule to a sorted set, and recurse with a dotted prefix for a nested record and an indexed prefix for list elements when the cascade marker is present.

fund-java/24-bean-validation-in-depth/02.instructions:
**Skills:** error responses · problem details · secrets in logs  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Our 400 responses are a stack trace for one client and an empty body for another. Design one error body for validation failures, and make sure it cannot leak a password."

**Why it matters.** A validation failure is the client's problem to fix, so the answer must say which fields failed and why, all at once. One stable shape (problem details with an `errors` map) lets every client render it. Echoing the rejected value helps with a quantity, but a password, token or card number in a response body ends up in logs and screenshots.

**Your task.** Implement `static Problem toProblem(List<Violation> violations)`:
- status 400, title `Invalid request`, detail `"1 field is invalid"` or `"<n> fields are invalid"` (n = distinct paths)
- `errors`: per path, its distinct messages sorted; paths in sorted order (a `TreeMap`)
- `rejected`: per path, the first invalid value as `String.valueOf`, except `"[redacted]"` when the path's last name (after the last `.`, without a trailing `[i]` index, lower-cased) contains one of `SECRET_WORDS` (so `passwordConfirmation` and `tokens[0]` count)
- an empty list is a programming error: `IllegalArgumentException`

**Worked example.** `[Violation("password", "size must be between 12 and 128", "hunter2")]` gives errors `{password: [size must be between 12 and 128]}` and rejected `{password: [redacted]}`.
hints: The client wants one entry per field, each listing what is wrong with it, and some fields must never show what was sent.

Collect messages per path into a sorted map without repeats, remember the first rejected value per path, and replace it with a placeholder when the last part of the path names a secret, ignoring case and any index.

Use a tree map from path to message list and another from path to value, skip a message already present, sort each list, take the name after the last dot without its index in lower case to decide redaction, and count the paths for the detail line.

fund-java/24-bean-validation-in-depth/03.instructions:
**Skills:** debugging · cascading validation · property paths  
**Level:** ★★★

**Bug hunt.** The code in the editor is a plausible first attempt at drill 1, "Build the validation walk: constraints, null rules and cascading". It passes some of the tests, but it has one real bug, the kind a reviewer should catch before it ships.

**Your task.** Find the bug and fix it, changing as little as you can; the tests are the same as drill 1's. The spec is unchanged: Implement `static List<String> validate(Record root)` for the given annotations (on record components). Return every violation as `"<path>: <message>"`, sorted:
- `@NotNull`: a `null` value gives `must not be null`
- `@NotBlank`: `null` or a blank string gives `must not be blank`
- `@Size(min, max)`: for a non-null value, its length (a `String`) or size (a `Collection`) outside `min..max` gives `size must be between <min> and <max>`
- `@Min(v)`: a non-null number below `v` gives `must be at least <v>`
- `@Valid`: for a non-null record, validate it with the path prefix `<name>.`; for a non-null list, validate each record element with the prefix `<name>[<index>].`
- the path of a component is its name, after any prefix
fund-java/24-bean-validation-in-depth/03.explanation: This validator cascades into a nested record marked `@Valid` but not into the elements of a `@Valid` list, so `items[1].sku` is never checked and an order with a blank SKU passes. That is the production bug from the interview prompt: the annotation is on the list, and nothing walks it. The test "each element of a @Valid list is validated, with its index in the path" catches it, and so do the four-item case, which expects `items[3].sku` among its three violations, and the zero-quantity boundary case. The nested-address test passes, because records still cascade. Add the list branch: validate each record element with the prefix `name[i].` instead of skipping the list.
hints: Nested objects are checked, yet one kind of container is not. Compare the two failing tests with the passing nested-record test.
A component marked for cascading may hold a record or a list of records. Look at which of the two the walk handles.
When the cascade marker is present and the value is a list, validate every record element with an indexed path prefix, the same way a nested record is validated.
